This book reproduces published figures, tables and results using `aggregate`. Every number in it is computed when the book is rendered. Nothing is transcribed from a previous run, so a match demonstrates the correctness of the current library version.

A library that computes compound distributions has to be correct. `aggregate` has an extensive set of *internal* correctness checks embodied in its validation system: these check for a match between the first three theoretical and empirical moments. However, a published number computed by somebody independent using a different method is a good *external* check. We work through results from twenty seven papers. Most of them confirm the library. Several of them correct it, or locate a limit in it that was not previously known. Seven of them turn out to contain an error, an internal inconsistency or a misprint, which is not a criticism of the authors so much as evidence that the check runs in both directions.

The first chapter is the short version: five papers, each with the DecL program that reproduces the published exhibit and the answer set beside the paper's own numbers. It takes ten minutes. Everything after it is the detail, which is the point of the exercise but not the place to begin!

## The shape of a chapter

Each chapter follows the same four structure: the context and the problem the paper is solving, the paper's own solution and the gold standard it publishes, the `aggregate` reproduction, and comments. A simple reproduction can be very short. Something unusual, or unfamiliar to actuaries, needs more context.

A chapter named for a paper that turned out **not** to be reproducible says so and gives the evidence. There is one, @Jin2016, and it has a part to itself. A negative result that explains precisely which feature is missing is more useful than silence, and in that case the missing feature is named: a common shock count mode for bivariate frequencies.

## Two kinds of paper

The papers fall into two groups, and what counts as success differs between them.

A **model paper** poses an insurance structure with explicit parameters. Reproduction means building it in DecL and matching the published numbers, and the paper is the authority. @Venter1983, @Mack2003, @Mata2005, @Bodoff2017, @Homer2003 and @Bear1990 are of this kind, and they make up the first part.

A **method paper** proposes a competing numerical technique for the aggregate distribution. Here `aggregate` is the exact ground truth against which the paper's own approximation is measured, so the roles reverse: the paper is the thing being checked. Whether reproduction is possible at all depends on whether the paper published concrete input parameters **and** tabulated output. Several rare-event papers publish neither, reporting only sample counts and CPU seconds, and that is a large part of why the later parts read the way they do.

A **theory paper** is a third kind, and the two @Denuit2025a and @Denuit2025 chapters are the instances. These prove things about the conditional expectation given the sum, $\mathsf E[X_i \mid S = s]$, and illustrate them with figures rather than tables. There is no insurance contract in either, and no compound distribution: each agent carries one claim with certainty, so what is under test is the allocation kernel and the grid it runs on. Success here means reproducing a *shape*, and it is checkable only because both papers state something numerical about the shape, a turning point in one case and a monotonicity failure in the other. Reproducing a figure is weaker evidence than reproducing a table, so these chapters lean on constraints the model must satisfy whatever the picture looks like: that shares add up, and that identically distributed agents get identical shares.

The two groups also arrived differently. The actuarial chapters come out of a candidate assessment that rated eighteen references from the author's library for suitability, tiering them by how well their worked examples map onto compound distributions, layers, reinsurance and risk measures. The numerical chapters come from a separate reading of the rare-event and convolution-accuracy literature, where the question was not "can this be reproduced" but "where does the FFT actually stop working".

## What came out of it

**The library is confirmed on its core.** @Venter1983's Exhibit 3 reproduces in all three columns, including the transformed gamma, which is `scipy.stats.gengamma` under a different name. @Bruno2006's Tables 6, 7 and 8 come back exact at every printed decimal. @Bodoff2017's Exhibit 4 reproduces cell for cell. @Homer2003 reproduces every published cell of sections 2 and 4, and 136 of the 147 cells of section 3. @Bear1990's Table I reproduces in both of its reproducible columns, six adjustable features priced by six DecL clauses.

**Four papers have errors the reproduction found.** @Mata2005's Table 1 limited expected values are not the exact lognormal ones, running 0.04% high at \$250,000 and drifting to 0.24% low at \$5M, while the closed form matches to eight figures. @Homer2003's Table 3.3 does not sum to one, carrying 99.97% of the mass, and those missing eleven cells are the consequence. @Asmussen2016a has a row where its two published saddlepoint columns and its Monte Carlo column disagree, and `aggregate`, being neither a saddlepoint expansion nor a sampler, can say which one to trust. @Denuit2025a's Figure 1 cannot hold at its right hand edge: agent 3's loss is capped at 30, so adding up forces agents 1 and 2 above 5 at a pool loss of 40, and their panels are drawn on an axis whose top tick is 4.

**The library has a floor, and these papers located it.** @BenRached2024's Theorem 3 predicts that FFT convolution error is bounded absolutely rather than relatively, so below roughly $10^{-13}$ the output is noise regardless of grid refinement. `aggregate` sits on that predicted floor to within a factor of a few. @Wilson2016a shows the same failure on adversarial inputs and, more usefully, shows that it is not always detectable: a wrong answer can come back positive and plausible. @Wilson2017 exhibits it on a benign input and demonstrates the repair. Together they turned a vague caveat into a measured property, and they are the reason the far tail now has documented limits rather than optimistic ones.

**Two working rules were recorded.** Check whether the paper's own tabulated inputs are exact before blaming a mismatch on `aggregate`, which is the lesson of @Mata2005. And put every limited expected value that will be *compared* with another onto a common grid, which is the lesson of @Mack2003.

## The chapters

| Chapter | Target | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| @Venter1983 | Exhibit 3, three methods over 34 rows | Reproduced. The bucket size selects which of the two exact columns you land on |
| @Mack2003 | Table 1, and the threshold above which Riebesell is exact | Reproduced. All 26 cells within 8e-4, and the threshold is $5.186\,\mathsf E[X]$ against the paper's "about 5" |
| @Mata2005 | Tables 1 to 14, trend and exposure adjustment by layer | Reproduced, and a discrepancy found in the paper's Table 1 |
| @Denuit2025a | Figure 1, the comonotonic repair of a conditional mean allocation | Reproduced, and the published figure cannot hold at its right hand edge |
| @Denuit2025 | Figures 2, 5 and 6, conditional expectation given the sum | Reproduced. The turning point lands at 64.46, which is what settles the index convention |
| @Denuit2019 | Figure 1 and the shares at $s = 1$, four participant pool | Reproduced. The horizontal line resolves a table that contradicts its own text |
| @Denuit2022b | Example 4.5, Figure 6, mortality credits at three pool sizes | Reproduced. Shares add up exactly at every pool size |
| @Wang2000 | Table 1, risk load by layer under two distortions | Reproduced to 0.31%, and the basic limit expected loss is misprinted |
| @Wang2002 | Table 2, weather derivative calls off 22 observations | Reproduced. Prices to under half a cent |
| @Gerber1982 | Tables 1 to 3, the exact stop loss premium columns | Reproduced. All 28 values inside the printed precision |
| @Robertson1992 | Table 4, the piecewise uniform algorithm | **Partial.** Exact for the paper, $O(h)$ for a lattice, so the printed precision is out of reach |
| @Embrechts1993 | Figure 1, discretization error and Richardson extrapolation | Reproduced. The $O(h^2)$ rate measured at 3.998 |
| @Grubel1999 | Tables 1 and 2, the L1 sums, the Theorem 2 bound | Reproduced, including the bound at 0.4641 |
| @Embrechts2009a | Table 1, three arithmetization designs | Reproduced **exactly**, all twelve values |
| @Schaller2008 | Table 4.3, operational risk quantiles | Reproduced to 2.2e-4, all twelve distinct values |
| @Bodoff2017 | Exhibit 4, excess of policy limits | Reproduced. Two unstated model choices inferred and confirmed by fit |
| @Homer2003 | All three worked examples of the bivariate FFT | Reproduced. Every construction is a shipped DecL form |
| @Bear1990 | Table I, six treaties with adjustable features | Reproduced. The lognormal column exactly, the collective risk column to the printed digit in five of six |
| @Bruno2006 | Tables 6, 7 and 8 | Reproduced exact at six decimals. 92,832 convolutions in seconds against the paper's 1,950 |
| @Wilson2016a | Table 2, the FFT-C columns | Reproduced. The finding is detectability, not error size |
| @Wilson2017 | The worst case, and its repair | Reproduced to the digit, and the repair demonstrated |
| @Asmussen2016a | Twelve tables, CDF and PDF | Reproduced from five build calls, and one bad row adjudicated |
| @BenAmar2023 | The seven probabilities the paper actually quotes | Reproduced. The whole left tail curve costs what one estimate costs them |
| @BenRached2024 | Table 6, and Theorem 3's floor | Reproduced, and the floor confirmed on the library itself |
| @Liu2026 | Tables 1, 2 and C.1 | Three of four reference points reproduced. The fourth is below the floor |
| Commentary | The rare-event group as a whole | Where these methods earn their keep, and where they do not |
| @Jin2016 | Nothing | **Not a reproduction.** The evidence, and the feature that would change it |

The final chapter is reference rather than reproduction: it records where each published severity curve shipped in `library.agg` came from, what the source paper uses it for, and every transcription decision behind the DecL.

## Reading and rebuilding

The chapters are independent. Read any one on its own. Two pairs reward being read together: @Homer2003 and @Jin2016 sit on opposite sides of the same feature boundary, dependence through a joint severity under a shared count against dependence through a common shock on the counts, and @Wilson2016a and @Wilson2017 are companion papers on the same failure, the first on adversarial inputs and the second on ordinary ones.

Rendering requires a Python environment with `aggregate` and its documentation extras installed, since every chapter executes. The two working documents in this folder, `README.md` and `plan-examples.md`, are notes rather than chapters and are deliberately outside the book: the first is a folder index and the second is the candidate assessment, which carries the tier ratings for the papers that were considered and rejected.
